content: 1. Management of Tuberculosis (TB) in Children: The National Tuberculosis Program (NTP) is responsible for implementing and managing TB care in children. This includes recording and reporting cases in two age groups: 0–4 years and 5–14 years. These practices are based on sound clinical and public health principles. 2. Definitions and Classification of TB Cases: A presumptive TB case refers to a patient presenting with symptoms or signs suggestive of TB. TB cases are classified based on: Anatomical site of disease (e.g., pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB). History of previous treatment. Drug resistance patterns. HIV status. A bacteriologically confirmed TB case is one where a biological specimen tests positive for TB using smear microscopy, culture, or WHO-approved rapid diagnostics (e.g., Xpert MTB/RIF). These cases must be reported regardless of treatment initiation. A clinically diagnosed TB case is one without bacteriological confirmation but diagnosed by a clinician based on clinical, radiological, or histological evidence. If bacteriological confirmation is later obtained, the case should be reclassified. 3. Pulmonary and Extrapulmonary TB: Pulmonary TB (PTB) involves the lung parenchyma or tracheobronchial tree and includes miliary TB. Extrapulmonary TB (EPTB) includes cases such as tuberculous lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion without lung involvement. Patients with both PTB and EPTB are classified as PTB. 4. History of Previous TB Treatment: New patients have never been treated for TB or have taken anti-TB drugs for less than one month. Previously treated patients have received at least one month of anti-TB drugs and are further classified based on the outcome of their most recent treatment: Relapse: Previously treated and declared cured or treatment completed, but now diagnosed with recurrent TB. Treatment after failure: Previous treatment failed. Treatment after loss to follow-up: Previously treated but lost to follow-up during their last treatment. Other previously treated patients: Outcome of prior treatment is unknown or undocumented. 5. HIV Status Classification: HIV-positive TB patients have a positive HIV test or documented evidence of HIV care enrollment. HIV-negative TB patients have a negative HIV test at the time of TB diagnosis. HIV status unknown applies to patients without HIV test results or documentation. If HIV status is later determined, the classification should be updated. 6. Drug Resistance Classification: Monoresistance: Resistance to one first-line anti-TB drug. Polyresistance: Resistance to more than one first-line drug, excluding both isoniazid and rifampicin. Multidrug resistance (MDR-TB): Resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin. Extensive drug resistance (XDR-TB): MDR-TB with additional resistance to fluoroquinolones and at least one second-line injectable drug. Rifampicin resistance (RR-TB): Resistance to rifampicin, with or without resistance to other drugs. 7. Treatment Outcome Definitions: Cured: A bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB patient who is smearor culture-negative in the last month of treatment and on at least one prior occasion. Treatment completed: Treatment finished without evidence of failure, but no bacteriological confirmation of cure. Treatment failed: Smear or culture remains positive at five months or later during treatment. Died: Patient dies before or during treatment. Lost to follow-up: Treatment interrupted for two consecutive months or more. Not evaluated: No treatment outcome assigned, including cases transferred out to another unit. 8. Tuberculin Skin Test (TST): Induration ≥5 mm is positive in HIV-positive or severely malnourished children. Induration ≥10 mm is positive in all other children, regardless of BCG vaccination status. 9. Sample Collection for TB Diagnosis: Expectoration: Children capable of producing sputum should do so in well-ventilated areas. Two specimens (on-the-spot and early morning) are recommended. Gastric aspiration: Used in young children who cannot produce sputum. Gastric contents are collected in the morning after fasting to maximize diagnostic yield. Sputum induction: Performed using nebulized hypertonic saline to stimulate sputum production. 10. Safety and Infection Control: Gastric aspiration is considered low-risk for TB transmission and can be performed at the bedside or in routine procedure rooms. Sputum induction, being aerosol-generating, requires specialized facilities and precautions. 11. Treatment Guidelines for Children: Interim guidelines recommend weight-based dosages of anti-TB drugs for children under 25 kg, using fixed-dose combinations (e.g., RHZ 60/30/150). This detailed explanation provides a comprehensive understanding of TB management in children, including diagnostic procedures, classifications, and treatment protocols.
